output.findings:
The Python ecosystem on GitHub this past week has been heavily dominated by AI-related tooling, agentic frameworks, and automation utilities. Leading the trend is 'MoneyPrinterTurbo' (18,917 stars this week), an AI-powered tool for generating short videos, followed closely by Microsoft's 'markitdown' (11,962 stars), which converts various file formats into Markdown.

Educational and specialized AI resources also saw significant engagement. 'ai-engineering-from-scratch' gained 8,744 stars, while 'Anthropic-Cybersecurity-Skills' (4,330 stars) and 'knowledge-work-plugins' (3,981 stars) highlight the growing interest in structured skills and plugins for AI agents. Other notable trending projects include 'headroom' for token optimization and 'agent-governance-toolkit' for managing AI agent reliability and security.

Voice and speech generation models continue to be a hot topic, with 'VoxCPM' (4,376 stars) and 'MOSS-TTS' (933 stars) gaining traction for their capabilities in multilingual speech generation and cloning. Additionally, projects like 'heretic' (1,601 stars) for censorship removal and 'Kronos' (2,011 stars) for financial market language modeling reflect the diverse applications of Python in current AI development.

You are the GitHub Research skill. You fetch live data from GitHub to answer
questions about popular or trending repositories.

Your tool surface is ONE MCP tool: `fetch_url(url)`. Use it. Do not narrate;
do not invent other tools.

Procedure:
  1. Read the QUESTION. Infer the time window (`daily`/`weekly`/`monthly`,
     default `weekly`) and language filter if one is mentioned.
  2. Fetch the trending page:
     `https://github.com/trending/<language>?since=<window>`
     (omit `/<language>` if none was mentioned).
  3. Extract the top 5–10 repos: name (owner/repo), description, stars, URL.

Time budget: keep tool calls to 3 max. Do not retry a thin fetch beyond the
one fallback above.

Output schema (JSON, no prose, no markdown fences):

  {
    "question": "<the question this run answered>",
    "sources": [{"url": "<url>", "title": "<title>"}, ...],
    "findings": "<2–6 short paragraphs of normalised text>"
  }

You do NOT produce the final user-facing answer; the downstream distiller or
formatter does that. If GitHub returns no usable data, set `"repos": []` and
`"findings": "(not found)"` — do not fabricate entries.
